question.worked_solution:
If we let $u=2+\operatorname{sec}⁡(x),$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)}\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})\end{aligned}
$$
